overview: Estonia proclaimed independence in 1918 and built schools, businesses and a parliamentary republic. Konstantin Päts imposed authoritarian rule in 1934. Soviet occupation in 1940 interrupted independence; this card follows the interwar state and its wartime disruption.

periods.title: An independent republic
periods.summary: Independence brought a constitution and elected government.

periods.title: Authoritarian government
periods.summary: Päts suppressed political competition after taking emergency powers.

periods.title: Occupation and war
periods.summary: Soviet occupation was followed by German occupation and the return of Soviet rule.

items.text: Compulsory schooling expanded from four classes in 1919 to six by 1930. Old schoolhouses became crowded as children stayed longer. A change in education law therefore meant very practical questions about desks, classrooms and space for another year’s pupils.

School architecture competitions in 1921 and 1930 offered communities new building plans. A fund established in 1922 provided long-term loans for construction and improvements. Hundreds of schools were built or modernized, making education a project involving builders as well as teachers.

Walter Zapp made a working prototype of the tiny Minox camera in Tallinn’s Nõmme district in 1936. Its small size required a new approach to the camera and its film. The design later entered factory production across the border in Riga.

One surviving 1936 Minox test photograph shows a girl at Pirita beach. Its negative measures only 9 by 6.5 millimeters. The museum preserves the image mounted on paper with Zapp’s signature: a very small piece of film with a remarkably large story.

Johannes Lorup’s new Tallinn glassworks opened in January 1934 with 180 employees. Glass melting continued around the clock, seven days a week, while workers rotated through three shifts. The furnaces had a much less relaxing bedtime routine than the people.

Lorup’s factory made ordinary milk bottles alongside elaborate table glass. In 1935 its workers’ association established a savings and assistance fund, supported by deductions from wages and contributions from management. It helped workers and families facing deaths or other emergencies.

Tartu opened as an Estonian-language university in December 1919. It initially lacked enough lecturers, so scholars came from Finland, Sweden and Germany. Building higher education in Estonian required both local expertise and international help.

The museum’s Härjapea farmhouse recreates the late 1930s home of the Orro family. Its orchard, flowerbeds and refurnished rooms show how farm households could combine earning a living with making a pleasant home. The holding had 44 hectares, including 13 hectares of fields.

Härjapea’s prosperous appearance did not mean electric light: electricity arrived only in the second half of the 1950s. Its late-1930s farmyard included a two-storey building combining pigsty, henhouse and fodder kitchen. Feeding the animals involved an entire little service complex.

At Lau village shop, business and family life shared one building. The shopkeeper had living rooms and a kitchen behind the selling and storage spaces. In 1938 and 1939 a tailor’s family rented another room and shared the kitchen. Work could be only a doorway from dinner.

Lau’s reconstructed 1938 stock includes garden tools, milk cans, kitchenware, thread, needles and groceries. Ceramic doll heads could be bought for making dolls at home. A village shop needed to help with cooking, repairs, farming and play, sometimes on the same shopping trip.

Estonian, section 1 of the 1920 constitution: “Eesti on iseseisev, rippumatu vabariik, kus riigivõim on rahva käes.” Translation: “Estonia is an independent, sovereign republic, where state power rests with the people.” The wording is preserved in the constitutional source collection.

ending.text: Soviet forces occupied Estonia in June 1940 and the USSR annexed it illegally. German occupation followed in 1941, then renewed Soviet occupation in 1944. Estonia’s legal continuity survived these occupations; independence was restored in 1991.
